title: Rapid Resistance Testing (RRT) protocol for Rapid Detection of Resistance to Carbapenems and Cephalosporins in Enterobacteriaceae Using Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry
author: Manal Tadros

steps_raw.instruction: Rapid Detection of Resistance to Carbapenems and Cephalosporins in Enterobacteriaceae Using Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry
Preparation of bacteria and antibiotic mixture for testing:
A sterile 1µl loop was used to suspend a fresh (18-24 hours old), pure colony of each isolate, at concentrations of 0.5 to 1.0 McFarland, in 2 milliliters of Mueller-Hinton broth.
Ampicillin, cefazolin, cefotaxime and imipenem all at individual concentrations of 0.5 µg/ml were added to the Muller-Hinton broth in which the bacteria were suspended.

An internal standard (oxazepam) was added to each tube at a final concentration of 40 ng/ml. The internal standard was included to correct for variations in extraction efficiency and LC-MS/MS performance.
The suspension of the bacteria with the mixture of antibiotics was incubated for one hour at 37˚C with gentle agitation at 200 cycles per minute in a shaking incubator.
Liquid Chromatographic (LC) Separation of Antibiotics:
A Shimadzu LC20 integrated high performance liquid chromatographic system (Shimadzu, Guelph, ON) was used in our study as follows:

300 µl of the suspension of each bacterial isolate and the antibiotic mixture was pipetted into an Eppendorf tube. 600 µl of absolute methanol was added and the mixture was briefly vortexed then centrifuged at 35,000x g in a mini-centrifuge for five minutes to remove precipitated protein
600 µl of the supernatant was pipetted into a 2 ml glass injection vial and mixed with 300 microliters of distilled LC grade water
The tubes were loaded to the LC for chromatographic separation.
Chromatographic separation was performed by passing the each mixture through a Phenomenex (Torrance, California) C-8 column (50mm x 4.6 mm)
Two solvents were used to facilitate the separation process; solvent A was composed of 5mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer (pH 7.0) and solvent B was methanol.
Chromatographic conditions:
Solvent flow rate was maintained at a rate of 1 ml/min with a starting condition of solution A 98% and solution B 2%
A series of stepwise linear gradients were used: 0-0.4 min. 65% solvent B, 0.4-1.3 min. 82% solvent B, 1.3-1.4 min. 98% solvent B
The flow was held from 1.4- 2.3 min. at 98% solvent B. At 2.3-3.3 min, the flow condition was stepped to 2% solvent B.
The entire chromatographic run for the mixture was completed in 3.3 minutes.
Tandem Mass Spectrometry to detect hydrolysis of the 4 antibiotics in the mixture:
Tandem mass spectrometry was performed on a Sciex 3200 Qtrap mass spectrometer (Sciex, Concord, ON) that was mated to the high performance liquid chromatographic system.
Electrospray ionization in the positive mode was achieved through a TurboIonSpray® source.

A standard curve was generated using 4 standards to facilitate quantitation; a blank standard (zero concentration of the 4 antibiotics), standard 1 with 0.25 µg/ml concentration of each of the four antibiotics, standard 2 and standard 3 with 0.5 µg/ml and 1 µg/ml concentration of each of the four antibiotics respectively.
Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) was used to quantify hydrolysis and improve

With regard to the MRM transitions: these were optimized by infusing each pure antibiotic (ampicillin, cefazolin, cefotaxime and imipenem) and also calculating the mono isotopic protonated mass of the major parent ion depending upon whether it is the entire molecule or whether it loses water or another functionality in source during ionization.

The daughter ions were chosen by doing fragmentation experiments on the chosen parent ion. Based on the initial experiments using pure antibiotics, the mass filter that would be selective for each antibiotic ion was selected in the first quadrupole (Q1).
Each selected ion then entered the second quadrupole (Q2) where it underwent collision-fragmentation.
The daughter ion specific to each parent ion was filtered selectively in the third quadrupole.
The specificity of the assay was based on the retention time in the liquid chromatography phase and the subsequent specific parent to daughter ion transition (MRM)

The recovered concentration of each parent drug in each tube was used to calculate the percent hydrolysis (ratio between the recovered drug recovered from the suspension of each bacterial isolate with the antibiotic mixture and the parent drug concentration determined from the standard plot.)

The internal standard ratio of each antibiotic to the oxazepam internal standard ensured accurate quantitation. All calibration standards were incubated in the same medium under identical conditions but without added bacteria.
Time requirements for performing the assay for a single bacterial isolate (Total: 1.5 hours):
1-	Bacterial preparation and incubation with the antibiotic mixture: 1hr 5 min
2-	Preparation for LC separation 15 min.
3- LC separation and MS/MS analysis 3.3 min.
4-	Integration and quantitation of antibiotics 10 min.
Each additional bacterial isolate would be incremented by 3.3 minutes which is the cycle time of the LCMS/MS.
